Consult Summary:
- 35-year-old male lawyer with several new symptoms since a recent job change: recurrent frontal headaches, decreased appetite with 5 lb unintentional weight loss, intermittent bilateral hand tingling, palpitations, shortness of breath at rest, feeling hot, and reduced libido.
- Patient has known hyperthyroidism on thyroxine; plan is in-person clinic assessment with cardiac/respiratory examination and thyroid blood tests prior to starting any new treatment.

Problem List:

Issue 1: Recurrent headaches
- Frontal headaches that come and go, predominantly during work (sitting at computer or meetings); began around time of job change.
- Associated symptoms: mild nausea during headaches.
- ROS pertinent negatives/positives: no aura or headache radiation reported beyond frontal area.
- Social/work: high stress at work (patient rates stress 7–8/10).
- Examination: no in-person exam documented.
- Specialist/allied review or differential: none performed; plan for in-clinic assessment.

Issue 2: Episodic paresthesia (tingling) in hands
- Intermittent tingling described as "quick picking" in both hands; first noticed since job change.
- Distribution: both hands, no leg involvement.
- Associated factors: occurs at work (example: when entering elevator in morning mentioned).
- Examination: no neurologic exam documented.
- Differential considerations not explicitly stated in consult.

Issue 3: Systemic symptoms possibly related to thyroid/cardiac effects
- Symptoms: feeling hot, intermittent shortness of breath while sitting at desk, palpitations (about once daily or more), decreased appetite, unintentional 5 lb weight loss, reduced libido — all onset since job change.
- Past medical history relevant: patient states he has hyperthyroidism and takes thyroxine.
- Medications/exam: taking thyroxine (dose/route/frequency not documented); no physical exam or vitals recorded.
- Plan discussed by doctor: in-person clinical review including heart and lung examination and blood tests for thyroxine level prior to changing medications.

Medications:
- Thyroxine — dose/route/frequency not documented.

Allergies:
- Patient reports no known allergies.

Past Medical History:
- Hyperthyroidism.

Social History:
- Occupation: lawyer, works in London.
- Work stress: reports high stress (7–8/10).
- Alcohol: drinks once weekly, a couple of glasses of wine.
- Smoking: denies smoking.
- Recreational drugs: denies use (specifically denied cocaine and marijuana).
- Living arrangements: not documented.

Preventative History:
- No preventive care items (cervical screen, mammogram, PSA, FOBT, BMD, vaccinations, optometry, skin check) documented in the consult.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: not documented.
- Examination findings: no in-person cardiac, respiratory or neurological exam documented; doctor recommended these be performed at clinic visit.

Plan:
- Book in-person appointment in clinic for physical examination (cardiac and respiratory exam) and documentation of vitals.
- Obtain blood tests for thyroxine (thyroid function tests) as discussed.
- No new medications to be started until in-person assessment and blood results.
- Patient to book clinic appointment via app; doctor will notify colleagues of presenting issues so patient need not repeat history.
- Further management and follow-up to be determined after clinic assessment and blood test results.

Document_quality:

- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Vitals (heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, temperature, oxygen saturation).
  - Results of any blood tests or thyroid function tests (tests were planned but results not available).
  - Dose/route/frequency of thyroxine (medication listed but details not documented).
  - Neurologic, cardiac, and respiratory examination findings.
  - ECG or other cardiac investigations (not documented; may be clinically expected given palpitations).
  - More detailed sexual/reproductive history and mental health assessment given decreased libido and work-related stress.

- Internal conflicts from the transcript:
  - None identified.

- Transcript quality:
  - Overall intelligible with some short pauses and minor fragmented phrases; sufficient to extract key clinical information.
